title: Architectural Genesis of FastMail
subtitle: How I Designed and Built this Desktop Email Client From Scratch

chapters.name: The Problem & Local Storage Foundation
chapters.problemStatement: Traditional webmail is slow, bloated, and unusable offline. I wanted an instant, keyboard-driven desktop email client that feels as fast as a local code editor. To achieve sub-millisecond search and offline reading, I needed a local-first SQLite database.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: I started by building `store.go`. I designed a normalized SQLite schema with tables for accounts, threads, messages, and attachments. I also added an FTS5 (Full-Text Search) virtual table so search queries execute in under 2ms without hitting the network.
authorRationale: Why SQLite? Zero setup, embedded, single-file storage in `~/.fastmail/mail.db` with sub-millisecond local reads.
Why FTS5? Enables instant tokenized full-text search over millions of email body words offline.
Why Parameterized Queries? Every query uses `?` placeholders to guarantee SQL injection safety.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created `LocalStore` struct and `NewLocalStore(dbPath)` with SQLite schema migrations.

chapters.name: Connecting to the Outside World: OAuth2
chapters.problemStatement: Now that I have local storage, I need to connect to real email providers (Gmail). Storing raw passwords in plaintext is insecure and violates OAuth standards. I needed a secure token handshake.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: I built `auth.go` with an `AuthService` struct. It implements Google's OAuth2 authorization code flow with offline access tokens and refresh tokens. When logging in, it spawns a temporary local loopback HTTP server to capture the redirect code, then encrypts and persists credentials in `~/.fastmail/tokens.json`.
authorRationale: Why local redirect server? Opens the user's default browser for Google sign-in and captures the OAuth callback on `localhost:8085` automatically.
Why refresh tokens? Access tokens expire after 60 minutes; refresh tokens allow silent background renewals without prompting the user.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created `AuthService` with `GetClient(account)` and browser OAuth authorization loops.

chapters.name: The Background Sync Engine & Concurrency
chapters.problemStatement: Fetching thousands of emails and attachments over network APIs takes time. If I run this synchronously on the main thread, the desktop UI will freeze. I needed high-concurrency background workers without crashing the app.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: I created `sync.go` with a dedicated `SyncEngine`. It uses background Goroutines to asynchronously poll Gmail API history deltas. To coordinate multi-account syncing safely, I added two distinct mutexes: `syncMu` (to prevent duplicate parallel sync jobs on the same account) and `mu` (to protect shared account state).
authorRationale: Why Goroutines? Go's lightweight green threads allow parallel mailbox syncing across multiple accounts with tiny memory footprint.
Why `syncMu` vs `mu`? `syncMu` protects long-running background sync operations, while `mu` is a quick RWMutex for reading active account state without contention.
Why Delta Tokens? Uses Gmail's `historyId` to fetch only new changes rather than re-downloading entire inboxes.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created `SyncEngine` with goroutine worker loops and delta synchronization.

chapters.name: Email Ingestion Security & Tracker Blocking
chapters.problemStatement: Emails from the internet are untrusted. Marketing emails contain invisible 1x1 tracking pixels (SendGrid, HubSpot, Mailchimp) that spy on when you open them, plus potentially malicious HTML scripts. I needed a privacy firewall.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: Before writing raw email bodies into SQLite, I pass them through `sanitizer.go` and `classifier.go`. `SanitizeEmailHTML` strips tracking images, removes dangerous script tags, and normalizes spacer bloat. `classifier.go` inspects headers to categorize emails into 'Main', 'Newsletters', and 'Updates'.
authorRationale: Why strip tracking pixels? Protects user IP and read receipts from senders.
Why auto-classification? Keeps personal conversations focused in 'Main' while newsletters and receipts are neatly split.
Design Note: While I started with regex-based stripping, upgrading to tokenized DOM parsing (`bluemonday`) will make it 100% immune to nested HTML mutations.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created `SanitizeEmailHTML` tracker filter and `ClassifyMessage` split inbox rule engine.

chapters.name: Desktop Orchestration & Wails IPC Bridge
chapters.problemStatement: I have the storage, auth, sync, and security layers. Now I need a central coordinator that binds all these Go services to native macOS/Windows window chrome and exposes a clean API to the web frontend.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: I created `app.go` and `main.go` using Wails v2. The `App` struct holds references to `LocalStore`, `AuthService`, and `SyncEngine`. Wails automatically generates TypeScript bindings for any exported method on `App`, and allows Go to emit reactive events (`wailsRuntime.EventsEmit`) directly to the frontend.
authorRationale: Why Wails over Electron? Wails uses the OS's native WebKit/WebView2, resulting in a 15MB binary instead of 200MB, with 10x lower RAM usage.
Why Typed IPC? Wails auto-generates TypeScript interfaces for all Go structs, eliminating runtime frontend/backend type mismatches.
Why Event Emitter? Background sync progress is pushed to the UI via `wailsRuntime.EventsEmit('sync:progress')`.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created `App` struct orchestrator and registered Wails IPC bindings in `main.go`.

chapters.name: The Reactive Svelte 5 User Experience
chapters.problemStatement: The backend is complete. The final step is building a modern, keyboard-driven UI with instant responsiveness, split inboxes, dark mode, and seamless message reading.
chapters.solutionArchitecture: I built the frontend in `frontend/src/App.svelte` using Svelte 5. It features a Superhuman-style 3-pane layout: Folders on the left, Thread List in the middle, and Message Reader on the right. Keyboard shortcuts (`j`/`k` for navigation, `e` for archive, `s` for star) allow navigating your entire inbox without touching the mouse.
authorRationale: Why Svelte? Zero virtual-DOM overhead, true reactivity, and instant DOM updates when emails sync in.
Why Keyboard First? Power users spend 80% less time processing emails when all actions have single-key bindings.
Why Split Inbox? Separates urgent emails from bulk newsletters without complex manual folder rules.
chapters.codeSnippetSummary: Created reactive Svelte 3-pane desktop layout with keyboard shortcut bindings.
